40:2.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “put on immortality” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and “put on incorruption” occurs in exactly two, both of them 1 Corinthians 15:53 and 15:54; “mortal must put on” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “there is no resurrection” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 22:23, Mark 12:18 and Acts 23:8, all of the Sadducees, and 1 Corinthians 15:12.
provenance.significance: Alma's sentence is built out of two consecutive strata of one KJV chapter and it uses them against each other. He opens with the Sadducees' formula — “there is no resurrection”, which in the KJV is only ever the denial of the resurrection party's opponents — and then converts the denial into a chronology by supplying Paul's own clauses as its content: this mortal does not yet put on immortality, this corruption does not yet put on incorruption. Recover 1 Corinthians 15 and the two halves are already in tension there: 15:12 is Paul asking how some among the Corinthians can say there is no resurrection, and 15:53 is his answer forty verses later. Alma states the error and the answer in one breath, and the pivot between them is the single word “until”. That is the whole rhetorical structure of the chapter — Corianton is not told he is wrong to be worried, he is told he has the timing wrong — and it is imported entire from a chapter written to answer the same worry.
provenance.alternative: 1 Corinthians 15:42-44, which supplies the corruption/incorruption pairing without the verb 'put on'; it is the stratum Alma 5:15 and 11:45 draw on.

40:2.note: The KJV's own words with the modal negated: 'this mortal does not put on immortality; this corruption does not put on incorruption, until after the coming of Christ.' 1 Corinthians 15:53 reads 'this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality', and the Book of Mormon reverses the order of the two clauses, substitutes the abstract 'corruption' for 'corruptible', and replaces 'must' with a denial governed by 'until'. Alma has used this chapter twice before (5:15, 11:45), both times paraphrasing it as 'raised in immortality … raised in incorruption'; this is the only place in the book where he uses Paul's actual verb, and the reason is that the argument here needs the verb's future tense in order to postpone it. Falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as one on the strength of the two KJV-pair phrases and the reproduced clause structure.

40:8.text: But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.

provenance.other: “one day is with the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:8. The Book of Mormon has 'with God' where Peter has 'with the Lord', so no run of words survives; what survives is the proposition and its function.
provenance.significance: Peter's sentence is not a remark about God's leisure but an answer to scoffers who ask 'where is the promise of his coming?' (3:4) — the delay of an appointed eschatological event is exactly what it is deployed to explain. Alma 40:8 deploys it for the same job in miniature: Corianton wants to know whether the dead rise at one time or several, and the answer is that the question is a creature of measured time, which is given to men and not to God. Recovering 2 Peter 3 also recovers what follows the sentence — 'the Lord is not slack concerning his promise' — which is the premise Alma needs in order to say that the interval between death and resurrection is not neglect. And the criterion that decides it is Hays's third, recurrence: Alma 41:1 borrows from 2 Peter 3:16 in the same letter, so the epistle is demonstrably in view and this verse is not being asked to carry the case alone.

40:8.note: 'All is as one day, with God; and time only is measured unto men.' The one KJV verse that equates a day with God's reckoning is 2 Peter 3:8, and Alma's second clause states the corollary Peter leaves implicit — that measurement is a human faculty. No run of words survives ('with God' for 'with the Lord'), and taken alone the sentiment is a commonplace available from Psalm 90:4 as well, which is why this was first weighed at moderate. What raises it is recurrence: the opening line of the next chapter, Alma 41:1, has 'some have arrested [1920: wrested] the Scriptures', and 'wrest' takes the scriptures as its object in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:16. The same short epistle-chapter stands behind a sentence early in Alma 40 and the first sentence of Alma 41, and 2 Peter 3 is throughout an argument about why a promised eschatological event has not yet happened — which is Corianton's question. Psalm 90:4 is about human transience and cannot account for the second borrowing.

40:11.text: Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

provenance.other: “God who gave” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 12:7, and “unto God who gave it” occurs in exactly one. The KJV elsewhere says 'the God of the spirits of all flesh' (Numbers 16:22, 27:16) and 'the Father of spirits' (Hebrews 12:9), neither of which has the relative clause.
provenance.significance: Alma is describing a doctrine he has just said was delivered to him by an angel, and the sentence he uses for it is Ecclesiastes'. The recovered context is awkward in a way that matters: Ecclesiastes 12:7 is the close of the Preacher's poem on old age and it is followed immediately by 'vanity of vanities'. Qoheleth's spirit returns to God as the terminus of a book that declines to say what happens next; Alma quotes the terminus and then spends fifteen verses saying what happens next. The borrowing converts the KJV's most reticent verse about the dead into the premise of the Book of Mormon's most detailed account of them, and the seam shows — 'taken home to that God who gave them life' adds both the destination-word 'home' and the object 'life', neither of which is in the verse, because Ecclesiastes' bare 'it' will not carry the weight.

40:11.note: 'The spirits of all men, whether they be good or evil, are taken home to that God who gave them life.' The relative clause is a KJV singleton and it belongs to the one verse in the Old Testament that tells the spirit where it goes at death. The Book of Mormon keeps the clause and changes what it is for: Ecclesiastes' 'the spirit shall return unto God who gave it' is a statement about dissolution, and Alma's is a statement about custody — the spirits are 'taken home', and the passive is the point, because the whole chapter turns on the dead being held somewhere by someone until an appointed time.

40:13.text: But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

provenance.route: Matthew 8:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Matthew 13:42's 'wailing' interpolated
provenance.other: “cast out into outer darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 8:12; the other two 'outer darkness' verses, Matthew 22:13 and 25:30, both read 'cast him into' or 'cast ye … into'. “weeping and gnashing of teeth” occurs in five KJV verses and “wailing and gnashing of teeth” in exactly two, Matthew 13:42 and 13:50, so the Book of Mormon's triple 'weeping, and wailing, and gnashing of teeth' is not a KJV reading at all: it is the two formulae welded together.
provenance.significance: A twelve-word run reproduced from the verse whose subject is 'the children of the kingdom' — that is, in Matthew, the people who had every right to expect to be inside and are not. Alma is answering a son who has assumed he is inside. The interpolated 'wailing' comes from Matthew 13:42, the furnace at the end of the parable of the tares, which is the KJV's other statement of the same sentence and which Alma 40:25 will quote from three verses later (Matthew 13:43). So the chapter's two Matthean borrowings are eleven verses apart in one parable-discourse: the wicked get 13:42's furnace-formula and the righteous get 13:43's shining forth, in the source's own order.

40:13.note: 'These shall be cast out into outer darkness; there shall be weeping, and wailing, and gnashing of teeth.' Twelve consecutive words of Matthew 8:12 with one word added, and the added word is the variant reading of the same sentence from Matthew 13:42. No KJV verse says 'weeping, and wailing, and gnashing of teeth'; the Book of Mormon's version is a conflation of the Gospel's two formulae, which is the signature of a writer quoting from a stock of remembered phrases rather than from a page.

40:13.text: Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished.

provenance.route: Matthew 12:43-45 / Luke 11:24-26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV calls a possessed person a 'house' in exactly one episode, told twice: Matthew 12:44 and Luke 11:24, where the unclean spirit says 'I will return into my house from whence I came out'. Elsewhere in the KJV a man's body is a 'tabernacle' (2 Corinthians 5:1, 2 Peter 1:13) or an 'earthly house' (2 Corinthians 5:1), never simply 'his house'.
provenance.significance: The Gospel episode ends 'the last state of that man is worse than the first', and 'state' is the word Alma 40 is organized around — the state of the soul, the state of happiness, the state of misery, 'thus they remain in this state'. Recover the source and the borrowed word 'house' arrives with the source's conclusion already attached: a spirit takes possession of a man's house, and what results is a state, and the state is a worse one. Alma 40:13 says all three things in one clause.

40:13.note: 'The spirit of the Devil did enter into them, and take possession of their house.' The metaphor of a person as the house a spirit enters and occupies is, in the KJV, the property of one episode — the unclean spirit who returns to 'my house from whence I came out' (Matthew 12:44, Luke 11:24) and brings seven worse with him. Held at moderate rather than higher because no phrase is shared: 'take possession' is not the Gospel's verb, and the figure is common enough in English devotional usage that Alma need not have had Matthew in view. What keeps it above an exclusion is that Alma's next word for the result is 'state', which is the word Matthew 12:45 ends the episode with.
40:13.whyNot: Zero verbal contact beyond the single word 'house'. A reader could reasonably say that a body inhabited by a spirit is called a house in any number of Christian sources and that the KJV is not needed to supply it.

40:13.text: Thou hast neither part nor lot in this matter: for thy heart is not right in the sight of God.

provenance.other: The KJV's 'no part nor —' frame occurs in six verses. Five are Deuteronomic and all read 'no part nor inheritance', of Levi's landlessness (Deuteronomy 10:9, 12:12, 14:27, 14:29, 18:1). The sixth is Acts 8:21, 'neither part nor lot', and it is the only one of the six in which what is denied is a share in the Spirit. “part nor portion”, the Book of Mormon's actual reading, occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Peter says it to Simon Magus, who has just tried to buy the giving of the Holy Ghost, and the ground he gives is a defect of the will — 'thy heart is not right in the sight of God'. Alma 40:13 denies the same thing on the same ground and in the same order: no part nor portion of the spirit of the Lord, 'for behold, they chose evil works, rather than good'. If the echo is real, what it carries over is not the phrase but Peter's diagnosis, that exclusion from the Spirit is a consequence of a choice already made and not an arbitrary sentence — which is the proposition Alma 40 and 41 exist to defend. The recurrence is the evidence. Acts 8:20-23 is a single speech of four verses, and the Book of Mormon has contact with three of them within a page: 8:20 at Mosiah 4:23 and 2 Nephi 9:30, 8:21 here, and 8:23 at Alma 41:11 by way of Alma's own conversion account. Simon Magus is the KJV's case of a man who wanted a spiritual gift on the wrong terms and was told his heart was the problem — which is the letter's diagnosis of Corianton throughout Alma 39-42.

40:13.note: 'They have no part nor portion of the spirit of the Lord.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which a man is told he has no part in the Spirit — Peter to Simon Magus — and its reasoning is Alma's reasoning: the ground given is a defect of the will, 'thy heart is not right in the sight of God', and Alma's is 'they chose evil works, rather than good'. On the wording alone this would sit at low, since 'part nor portion' is in no KJV verse and the 'no part nor —' frame is five-sixths Deuteronomic boilerplate. It is held at moderate because of recurrence: Alma 41:11, three verses of running argument later, quotes Acts 8:23 — 'the gall of bitterness, and in the bonds of iniquity' — from the same speech of Peter's, two verses on from this one. Peter's rebuke of Simon Magus is demonstrably in view across Alma 40-41, and that is what makes 40:13's fainter contact worth proposing.
40:13.whyNot: The Book of Mormon's noun matches no KJV verse, and the 'no part nor —' frame is common enough (six verses, five of them Deuteronomic boilerplate about Levi) that it identifies nothing on its own. A reasonable reader will call this an independent English idiom and decline the link; it is filed at low, with the argument, rather than buried in the register, because the contextual fit at Acts 8:21 is exact and worth putting in front of someone.

40:14.text: But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.

provenance.other: “fearful looking for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “fiery indignation” occurs in exactly one; both are Hebrews 10:27, and the two phrases stand four words apart there. “devour the adversaries” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'of the wrath of God' for the KJV's 'of judgment', and 'wrath of God' occurs in ten KJV verses.
provenance.significance: Two absolute singletons from one clause, in the source's order, and the n-gram stream missed the verse entirely because the Book of Mormon interposes 'awful' between them. What the recovered context supplies is the condition Hebrews attaches: 10:26 has 'if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins' — that is, the fearful looking-for is specifically the prospect of those who knew better. Corianton knew better; Alma 39 has just said so at length. Hebrews 10:27 is the KJV's sentence for exactly the person Alma is writing to, and it arrives in this chapter as the state of the wicked dead between death and resurrection — a waiting, which is what Hebrews' 'looking for' means and what the whole chapter is about.

40:14.note: 'A state of awful, fearful looking for of the fiery indignation of the wrath of God upon them.' Two KJV singletons, both from Hebrews 10:27, in the KJV's own sequence, with 'awful' inserted and 'of judgment' exchanged for 'of the wrath of God'. Neither phrase exists anywhere else in the KJV, so the verse is not merely the best candidate but the only one; and the borrowing is doing work, because 'looking for' is a word of expectation and Alma needs the wicked dead to be waiting rather than already punished.

40:16.text: But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection.

provenance.other: “the first resurrection” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 20:5 and 20:6, and nowhere else in scripture. The New Testament has no other name for a resurrection prior to a general one.
provenance.significance: Alma introduces the term as something already in circulation — 'again it hath been spoken, that there is a first resurrection' — and then spends five verses arguing about what it can and cannot mean. That is a term being received rather than coined, and there is exactly one place in the KJV to receive it from. Recovering Revelation 20 recovers the shape of the dispute as well: John's first resurrection is separated from the rest of the dead by an interval ('the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished'), and an interval between two resurrections is precisely the problem Corianton has raised and Alma is solving. What Alma does with it is characteristic — he denies the reading that makes the first resurrection a resurrection of souls only (40:17) and insists it is a reuniting of soul and body (40:18), which is an exegetical decision taken about a phrase, in the manner of a commentator.

40:16.note: 'Again it hath been spoken, that there is a first resurrection.' The phrase is a KJV two-verse phrase confined to Revelation 20:5-6, and Alma quotes it as received terminology and then adjudicates its sense. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Revelation 20:5-6 here. The chapter goes on to draw on the same chapter of Revelation again at 40:21, in the source's own order — the first resurrection at 20:5-6, then judgment 'according to their works' at 20:12-13.

40:21.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “according to their works” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: 2 Corinthians 11:15, Revelation 20:12 and Revelation 20:13. Alma 40:21 also has 'stand before God', which in the KJV occurs at Revelation 20:12 and, in the singular, at Luke 1:19.
provenance.significance: Two clauses of one KJV verse — standing before God and being judged according to their works — arrive together and in the source's order. What makes this more than the book's standing formula is where it sits: five verses earlier Alma has taken 'the first resurrection' from Revelation 20:5-6, and here he takes the judgment scene from Revelation 20:12-13. He is moving through John's chapter in John's sequence, and John's sequence is exactly the sequence Corianton's question requires — first the resurrection, then the interval, then the books. Recovering Revelation 20 supplies the one element Alma withholds: John's dead are judged out of written books, and Alma 41, immediately following, will replace the books with a man's own restored disposition.

40:21.note: 'Brought to stand before God, and be judged according to their works.' This formula is Alma's settled way of naming the judgment and has already been adjudicated at Alma 3:26 and 11:41-44, so on the ordinary rule (ADJUDICATING §4) a fourth occurrence would go to the register rather than get a row. It gets a row because the argument here is the sequence, not the phrase: Alma 40 reaches Revelation 20:12-13 five verses after reaching Revelation 20:5-6, in the order John has them, and a reader shown the first resurrection at 40:16 and then shown nothing at 40:21 has been told the chapter's dependence on Revelation 20 stopped where it in fact continues.

40:23.text: But there shall not an hair of your head perish.

provenance.other: “hair of your head” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:18, and “hair of his head fall” occurs in exactly one, 1 Samuel 14:45. The idiom as a whole is spread across some seven verses (1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:11, 1 Kings 1:52, Daniel 3:27, Luke 12:7, 21:18, Acts 27:34), and the verb the Book of Mormon uses — 'lost' — is in none of them.
provenance.significance: In the KJV the not-a-hair formula is always a promise about a living body in danger: Jonathan under Saul's oath, Absalom's messenger, the three men out of the furnace, Paul's shipmates before the wreck. Alma applies it to a body that has already dissolved, and makes it a promise about reassembly rather than preservation. Luke 21:18 is the one occurrence in an eschatological discourse, and the sentence that immediately follows it is 'In your patience possess ye your souls' — a verse about keeping possession of the soul, standing next to a verse about keeping the hairs of the head, in a chapter about the end. That is the pair Alma 40:23 needs, and it is the pair Luke has.

40:23.note: 'Even a hair of the head shall not be lost, but all things shall be restored to its proper and perfect frame.' The idiom is biblical and its exact wording here is not: the KJV's hairs perish, or fall to the ground, or are singed, and none of them is 'lost'. Luke 21:18 is proposed as the head of the composite because it is the only occurrence in an end-of-the-world discourse and because Luke 21:19 immediately couples it with possessing one's soul, which is the chapter's subject. 1830 reads 'restored to its proper and perfect frame' where 1920 reads 'their'; the singular is the older grammar and does not bear on the source.
40:23.whyNot: The formula is distributed across seven KJV verses and is an ordinary English idiom besides; no single verse can be shown. A reader may reasonably treat this as the Book of Mormon using a proverb rather than quoting a text, in which case the composite is the honest answer and Luke's headship is an inference from context alone.

40:25.text: Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

provenance.other: “then shall the righteous shine forth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:43; “shine forth” occurs in three (Job 11:17, Psalm 80:1, Matthew 13:43) and in neither of the others is the subject the righteous. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Alma 40:25 against Daniel 12:3, which Matthew 13:43 is drawing on, and against Matthew 13:43, and returns one decisive point for Matthew: the Book of Mormon has the kingdom where Daniel has 'brightness of the firmament'. No word of Daniel 12:3 survives in the Book of Mormon's sentence.
provenance.significance: Alma quotes the clause and drops the simile — 'as the sun' is gone — and changes the destination from 'the kingdom of their Father' to 'the Kingdom of God'. Both changes point the same way. Matthew's sentence is the closing line of the explanation of the parable of the tares, spoken to disciples in private, and it ends with the formula 'Who hath ears to hear, let him hear'; the two verses before it are the furnace and the wailing and gnashing of teeth that Alma has already used at 40:13. So the chapter takes its picture of the wicked dead from Matthew 13:42 and its picture of the righteous dead from 13:43, twelve verses apart in the dossier's reckoning but consecutive in the Gospel, and in the Gospel's own order. What Alma removes is the parable's frame: Matthew is describing the harvest at the end of the world and Alma is describing the state of a soul after the resurrection.

40:25.note: 'And then shall the righteous shine forth in the Kingdom of God.' Six of Matthew 13:43's first seven words, and the seven-word opening 'then shall the righteous shine forth' is a KJV singleton. The excisions are as informative as the quotation: the simile 'as the sun' goes, and 'of their Father' becomes 'of God', which is the form Alma uses throughout this letter. The verse pairs with 40:13, which takes 'wailing' from Matthew 13:42 — the immediately preceding verse — so the whole of Alma's final antithesis, wicked then righteous, is Matthew 13:42-43 read in order.

40:26.text: For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them.

provenance.other: “dregs” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17 and 51:22. Isaiah's are the cup of trembling taken out of Jerusalem's hand and given to her afflicters; Psalm 75:8 is the only one in which it is the wicked who drink them. “bitter cup” occurs in no KJV verse. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Alma 40:26 against Psalm 75:8 and Revelation 14:10 — the New Testament's reworking of the same cup, 'the wine of the wrath of God … poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation' — and returns one decisive point for the Psalm, on the dregs-drinking clause that Revelation does not have.
provenance.significance: The Psalm's cup is a cup of judgment held in God's hand, and its sting is that the wicked do not merely receive it, they 'wring them out, and drink them' — they take the last of it themselves. That is the exact figure Alma needs for the sentence he has just written: the wicked are 'consigned to partake of the fruits of their labors or their works, which have been evil'. The judgment is self-administered. Recovering Psalm 75 makes the point sharper still, because 75:7 is 'God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another' — a verse about God allotting, immediately before a verse about the wicked serving themselves; the psalm holds together the two things Alma 40:26 and the whole of Alma 41 are trying to hold together, that God judges and that the sinner brings it on himself.

40:26.note: 'They drink the dregs of a bitter cup.' The KJV has dregs in three verses and only Psalm 75:8 has the wicked drinking them, from a cup in the hand of the LORD. Revelation 14:10 takes over the same cup but loses the dregs — it reads 'without mixture' where the Psalm reads 'full of mixture' — so the mediation runs through the Old Testament and not the New. 'Bitter cup' is the Book of Mormon's own addition and appears in no KJV verse; the adjective is doing what the Psalm's 'wine is red' does, and it is worth noting that the Book of Mormon will give the same cup to Christ at 3 Nephi 11:11.
